2 mega-cap stocks with exciting potential and 1 we avoid

Megacap stocks dominate their sectors and their actions influence economies worldwide. The flip side though is that their sheer size means they have less room for explosive growth as scale works against them.

Sound complicated? With StockStory, it doesn't have to be. Our job is to find you high-quality companies that can win regardless of the conditions. Keeping that in mind, here are two industry titans with attractive long-term potential and one that could be stalling.

One mega-cap stock to sell:
Walmart (WMT)

Market cap: $962 billion

Known for its large-format Supercenters, Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) is a retail pioneer that serves a budget-conscious consumer who is looking for a wide range of products under one roof.

Why Are We Wary of WMT?

The company has faced growth challenges as its 5.3% annual revenue increases over the last three years fell short of other consumer retail companies

Widely-available products (and therefore stiff competition) result in an inferior gross margin of 24.9% that must be offset through higher volumes

Responsiveness to unforeseen market trends is restricted due to its substandard operating margin profitability

Walmart's stock price of $123.24 implies a valuation ratio of 39.5x forward P/E. If you're considering WMT for your portfolio, see our FREE research report to learn more.

Two mega-cap stocks to watch:
Microsoft (MSFT)

Market cap: $3.94 trillion

Originally named "Micro-soft" for microcomputer software when founded in 1975, Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) is a global technology company that develops software, cloud services, devices, and AI solutions for consumers, businesses, and organizations worldwide.

Why Should You Buy MSFT?

Microsoft is one of the great brands not just in tech but all of business. It produces mission-critical software and bundles it together, resulting in cream-of-the-crop gross margins.

The company's elite unit economics lead to robust profit margins that improve over time. This speaks to the scale advantages and operating efficiency across its diverse portfolio, which spans everything from Office and Azure to Minecraft.

Microsoft has a virtuous cycle of returns. Its dominant market position enables it to generate strong free cash flow, and it reinvests these funds into promising ventures that further strengthen its competitive moat.

title: AMD Reports on Nov. 3. Here's What You Should Do Before Then.
detail:
AMD Reports on Nov. 3. Here's What You Should Do Before Then.
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 30, 2026 at 11:50 AM EDT 4 min read
AMD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Earnings for Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ: AMD) are right around the corner. This can be a tumultuous time in the stock market, as companies can either exceed expectations and soar, or miss them and plummet. The risk becomes even higher when stocks are highly valued, like AMD is, as it must blow expectations out of the water to justify its current valuation.

As a result, I think investors should consider taking action before Nov. 3 (when AMD reports), because the stock has a very high valuation that may be tough to live up to. Here's why.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
AMD's stock is very pricey

AMD's shares have had an incredible year, rising nearly 150% so far. However, the business hasn't been growing nearly that fast (although its earnings have).

AMD EPS Diluted (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts.

AMD's margins are dramatically improving, which is driving the strong earnings growth. However, some of that growth should go to offsetting its expensive stock price, as it trades at a ridiculous price tag of 136 times trailing earnings.

AMD PE Ratio data by YCharts.

Industry rival Nvidia trades for about 27 times earnings, which I think is a fair price tag. For AMD to fall to 30 times earnings, either the stock price would have to collapse (I don't think it will), or it must increase its earnings by about 350%.

The market is bullish on it getting that done, because its stock trades for 34 times next year's earnings estimates. So, that tells investors that there's basically a year and a half worth of very strong growth already baked into the stock price.

That's a steep price to pay for a stock like AMD, especially one that isn't the industry leader (Nvidia is). I think this reality could set in following a third-quarter (Q3) earnings announcement. Investors will begin to realize how expensive AMD's stock is and how cheap Nvidia's is, and rotate from one into the other. This could ignite a major sell-off as investors race to take gains and find the next biggest stock before 2027 arrives.

AMD's stock has gotten in front of itself. While the company has made up some ground in the artificial intelligence (AI) arms race, it's still not nearly enough to be a huge challenger to Nvidia. Nvidia is still growing at a much faster pace overall (106% in Q2 versus 50% for AMD), underscoring that it's still the top dog in the industry. While AMD's stock price assumes that it has outright won the AI computing unit battle, that's far from the case, and AMD shareholders need to be cautious as a result.
